prime.problem: A lock lets exactly one thread in. Real limits are often "at most 3 downloads", "at most 10 connections" or "wait until an item exists". Counting those with a shared integer is a check-then-act race, and waiters end up polling. You need a counter whose check and decrement happen as one step, and that puts waiters to sleep.
prime.fits: Third Synchronization card. It generalises the lock (a semaphore at 1) and drops the mutex's ownership, which is what lets one thread signal another. Monitors (next) replace counters with arbitrary conditions.
expect: limiting concurrency: 10 downloads, 3 at a time
the bounded buffer with two semaphores
prime.goal: Pick the initial count for a lock, a limit and a signal; trace the counter through the download and bounded-buffer examples; and spot the mutex-before-P deadlock.

attend: What do starting values 1, 3 and 0 turn a semaphore into, and why does the same P/V code serve all three?
In the download trace at 0.1 s, why does the counter stay at 0 even though three downloads just finished?
In the bounded buffer, what do free and full each count, and why does free + full stay at 2?
Why does taking the buffer's mutex before P(free) deadlock, when taking it after is fine?
What does a BoundedSemaphore catch that a plain one silently allows?

must: A counter of permits whose P (check + decrement) is atomic → no two threads can both see "one left" → at most s₀ threads between P and V → Semaphore(3) capped 10 downloads at 3 in flight
P on 0 sleeps; V wakes one sleeper → waiters use no CPU and each V lets exactly one through → 10 downloads run in ceil(10/3) = 4 waves → 0.4 s ideal, 0.416 s measured

No owner: any thread may V → a semaphore can signal between threads (start at 0: one P's, another V's) → two semaphores count empty and full slots → producer and consumer each sleep exactly when they must (bounded buffer)
Semaphores encode conditions as counts → correctness depends on the order of P's and locks → taking the mutex before P(free) lets the producer sleep holding what the consumer needs → deadlock
elevated: Python's counter never goes below 0, while OSTEP's goes negative to count waiters → same behaviour, different bookkeeping → when reading OSTEP's traces, −k means k threads asleep
reference: Dijkstra's names P (proberen) and V (verhogen), and EWD123
the exact start-time list and the 0.016 s overhead

compress.prompt: From memory, write the P and V rules and the invariant, then reproduce the download timeline (counter, running, waiting) at 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 s. Finally, write the producer's and consumer's three lines in the right order and mark the ordering that would deadlock.
checklist: P: if s > 0 decrement and go, else sleep; V: increment and wake one
check and decrement are one atomic step
bounded buffer: P(free) put V(full); P(full) get V(free); mutex only around the buffer

retrieve.q: Explain why a semaphore can be used as a signal between two threads but a mutex can't.
answer: a semaphore has no owner: any thread may V, even one that never P'd
start at 0: the waiter's P sleeps until the other thread's V
a mutex must be released by the thread that locked it, so it can't carry a signal from another thread

retrieve.q: Walk the bounded buffer (capacity 2) through put a, put b, put c with a consumer that hasn't started: give free, full and who is asleep after each step.
answer: put c: the producer's P(free) finds 0 and sleeps; free 0, full 2
it wakes only when the consumer's get does V(free)

retrieve.q: You must cap outbound API calls at 3 in flight. Compare one lock, no limit, a shared if running < 3 check and Semaphore(3) for 10 calls of 0.1 s.
answer: one lock: correct but serial, 1.0 s
no limit: 0.1 s, until the load is large enough to break the server or rate limit
shared check: check-then-act race, 4 can run, and waiters must poll
Semaphore(3): about 0.4 s (0.416 measured), never more than 3

compare.q: The bounded buffer built from two semaphores vs from a lock and two condition variables: what does each encode the "not full" condition as, which design choice makes one easier to get wrong, and when would you pick the semaphore version?
answer: semaphores: as counts (free slots, full slots); conditions: as a test while len(buf) == CAP under the lock
semaphores rely on the order of P's and the mutex, so a swapped order deadlocks; conditions re-check any predicate under one lock
pick semaphores when the condition really is a count (a pool of N, a limit); pick conditions for predicates that aren't counts

compare.q: Semaphore(3) around downloads and backpressure in a service both cap work in flight. What does each protect, and what happens to the excess in each?
answer: both keep a downstream resource from being overwhelmed
the semaphore makes excess threads sleep in line; backpressure refuses or slows excess requests upstream
a waiting queue that grows without bound is the failure both try to avoid

predict.q: Same 10 downloads of 0.1 s, but now Semaphore(4). Then Semaphore(5). Predict the wall time of each and the counter's value at the moment the last download starts. Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Semaphore(4): ceil(10/4) = 3 waves, about 0.3 s. Semaphore(5): 2 waves, about 0.2 s. With 4 permits the last wave has 2 downloads, so when it starts the counter is 4 − 2 = 2 after the other two permits come back; with 5 permits the second wave is full and the counter is 0. Past 5, more permits can't beat 2 waves until you reach 10 (1 wave, 0.1 s).

apply.task: Modify code/semaphores.py: run the 10 downloads with Semaphore(1), (2), (3), (4), (5) and (10) and record wall time and max in flight. Then deliberately swap the producer's order to with mutex: around free.acquire() and the append, run it with acquire(timeout=1) on free, and record what happens.
apply.done: Your six timings sit near the computed waves (1.0, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 s), max in flight never exceeds the permit count, and the swapped version times out once the buffer fills, because the consumer is blocked on the mutex the producer holds.
